entries.definition: A small entry space with two interlocking doors where only one opens at a time, so a person can be checked before reaching the secure area and tailgating is prevented.
Gathering information about a target by directly interacting with its systems, such as port scanning or probing services, which can be detected.
A Zero Trust approach that adjusts how much verification a sign-in needs based on real-time context such as location, device health and behaviour, rather than trusting a fixed credential alone.
Physical isolation of a system or network from all other networks, including the internet, so data can move in or out only by deliberate manual means.
Adjusting monitoring rules and thresholds to reduce false positives and noise while still catching genuine threats, so analysts can focus on meaningful alerts.
Training users to notice and report actions that are risky, unexpected or unintentional, by themselves or others, that may signal a security problem.
Labelling hardware with a unique identifier, such as a barcode or RFID tag, linked to an inventory record so ownership, location and lifecycle can be tracked.
The total set of points, such as open ports, services, interfaces and users, where an attacker could try to enter or extract data from an environment.
Formal evidence-backed confirmation that something is as claimed, such as a device proving its integrity before access or an auditor certifying that controls are in place.
A documented, pre-tested set of steps for reversing a change and restoring the previous working state if the change fails or causes unexpected problems during implementation.
A cryptographic attack exploiting the probability that two different inputs will produce the same hash far sooner than expected, used to find collisions in weak hashing algorithms.
Unnecessary software preinstalled by a device maker or vendor that wastes resources and can widen the attack surface with unpatched or insecure components.
Pretending to be a well-known company, by copying its logos, emails or websites, to trick people into trusting a malicious message, payment request or login page.
A flaw where a program writes more data into a memory area than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially letting an attacker crash it or run their own code.
A program offering rewards to outside researchers who find and report vulnerabilities in an organisation's systems under defined rules.
A fraud in which attackers take over or convincingly spoof an executive's or supplier's mailbox to trick staff into wiring money, changing bank details or sending sensitive data.
Forecasting the people, technology and infrastructure needed to keep services running under expected and peak demand, including during a disruption.
A documented record of everyone who handled a piece of evidence, when and why, proving it was not tampered with so it remains admissible in court.
Grouping multiple servers so they work together and appear as one system; if a node fails, another takes over its workload, providing high availability.
Digitally signing software with a developer's certificate so users and systems can confirm who published it and that it was not altered after release.
A recovery location with space, power and connectivity but no ready equipment or current data; cheapest to maintain but slowest to bring into service.
An alternative safeguard put in place when the primary required protection cannot be implemented, reducing the risk to an acceptable level by other means, such as isolating an unpatchable system.
Packaging an application with its dependencies into a lightweight isolated unit that shares the host's kernel, letting workloads run consistently and separately on one system.
The incident response phase that limits an attack's spread, for example by isolating infected hosts or disabling accounts, before the threat is removed.

In Zero Trust, the layer that makes access decisions, using the policy engine and policy administrator to evaluate requests and instruct enforcement points, separate from where user traffic actually flows.
A safeguard that acts after an incident to limit damage and restore systems to normal, such as restoring from backup or removing malware once it has been found.
Capturing valid authentication data, such as a session token or login exchange, and resending it later to impersonate the user without ever knowing the actual password.
Information stored on a medium such as a disk, database or backup tape, protected mainly by encryption, permissions and physical security.
The organisation that determines why and how personal data is processed and bears primary legal responsibility for protecting it.
The role responsible for the day-to-day technical handling of data, such as storage, backups and applying access controls, as directed by those accountable for it.
Information moving across a network between systems, protected mainly by encrypted protocols such as TLS or IPsec tunnels.
Information currently being processed in memory or by the CPU, which is hardest to protect and may rely on techniques like secure enclaves.
Obscuring part or all of a sensitive value, for example showing only the last four digits of a card number, so people and test systems can work with data without seeing the real contents.
The senior person accountable for a specific dataset, who decides its classification and who may access it.
In Zero Trust, the layer where subjects actually reach resources and traffic is carried, governed by enforcement points that apply the decisions made elsewhere.
An entity that handles personal data on behalf of, and under the instructions of, the organisation that decides why it is processed, such as a payroll service.
Rules defining how long specific types of data must be kept, and when it must be disposed of, to meet legal, regulatory and business needs.
The principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected or stored, affecting where organisations may keep and process it.
The individual whom personal data describes or identifies, who holds privacy rights over that information under laws such as GDPR.
Exposing magnetic storage media to a powerful magnetic field to erase its contents, which also typically renders hard drives unusable; ineffective on SSDs.
A safeguard that identifies and records suspicious activity while or after it happens, such as log reviews, motion sensors or intrusion alerts, without necessarily stopping it.
A safeguard meant to discourage an attacker from trying at all, such as warning signs, visible cameras or login banners, by making an attack seem risky or unrewarding.

A value created by encrypting a message's hash with the sender's private key; anyone holding the public key can verify who sent it and that it was not altered, supporting integrity and non-repudiation.
A safeguard that tells people what they must or must not do, such as a policy, procedure or posted instruction, relying on compliance rather than technical enforcement.
Forcing two parties to fall back to an older, weaker protocol or cipher suite during negotiation so the attacker can then break or intercept the connection.
Acting as a reasonable, prudent organisation would by implementing and maintaining appropriate safeguards, demonstrating that responsibilities are actually being carried out.
The investigation and research done before a decision, such as vetting a vendor's security and finances, to understand risks before entering an agreement.
The process of identifying, collecting and producing electronically stored information requested as evidence in a lawsuit or investigation.
A dedicated computer built into a device to perform a specific function, such as in medical equipment or vehicles, often hard to patch and limited in security features.
Short-lived access credentials generated for a single task or session and automatically expiring afterward, so there is no standing secret to steal.
The incident response phase that removes the root of the threat, such as malware, backdoors and compromised accounts, after it has been contained.
A formally approved, usually temporary permission to deviate from a policy or fix requirement for a specific case, typically with compensating controls and a review date.
A formal release from having to meet a requirement at all, granted by an authority for a system or group, generally longer-lasting than a one-off approved deviation.
The percentage of an asset's value expected to be lost if a particular threat succeeds, used with asset value to calculate single loss expectancy.
An independent examination of an organisation's controls and records performed by an outside party, giving stakeholders and regulators objective assurance.
A failure mode where a security device blocks all traffic when it malfunctions, preserving security at the cost of availability.
Behaviour in which a crashed or unpowered security appliance keeps passing traffic without inspection, so the business stays online but unfiltered traffic gets through.
A result where a scanner or detection system fails to flag a real vulnerability or attack, leaving a genuine problem unnoticed.
A result where a scanner or detection system reports a problem or attack that does not actually exist, wasting analyst time.
A trust arrangement between separate organisations or domains that lets users authenticate with their home identity provider and access partner resources without separate accounts.
A comparison of an organisation's current security posture against a target framework or desired state, used to identify missing or weak controls and prioritise improvements.
Placing data centres and backup sites far enough apart that a single regional disaster, such as a flood or power outage, cannot take them all down.
Determining the physical location of a device or user from IP address, GPS or other signals, used to enforce region-based access rules and spot suspicious sign-ins.
Automated policy checks built into processes and pipelines that prevent people or scripts from making insecure changes, while still letting them work quickly.
An attacker motivated by a political, social or ideological cause, who uses defacement, leaks or denial of service to draw attention to their message rather than for profit.
Reducing a system's attack surface by removing unneeded services, closing ports, changing defaults and applying secure settings and patches.
A one-way function that turns input of any length into a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the output, so it is used to verify integrity and store passwords.
Designing systems with redundancy and no single point of failure so services stay up for a very high percentage of the time, often measured in nines.
A decoy document with an enticing name, such as passwords.txt, placed on a system and monitored so that any attempt to open it signals unauthorised activity.
A whole network of decoy systems and services built to look like a real environment, used to observe attacker behaviour across multiple machines and keep intruders away from production.
A single decoy system deliberately made attractive to attackers, used to detect intrusions, waste attackers' time and gather intelligence on their tools and techniques.
A fake piece of data, such as a bogus credential, API key or database record, planted so that its use or appearance anywhere reveals a breach and possibly its source.
A fully equipped recovery facility with current data and running systems that can take over operations almost immediately; fastest but most expensive option.
Verifying that a person really is who they claim to be, for example by checking government ID, before an account or credential is issued to them.
A review performed before approving a change to determine what systems, users and processes it could affect and what risks it introduces, informing whether and how to proceed.
An area of a network where traffic is assumed to be safe once inside; Zero Trust aims to shrink or eliminate these so every request is still evaluated.
An indicator where one account signs in from two distant locations within a time too short for physical travel, suggesting stolen credentials or shared access.
An evaluation of a vendor's security carried out by a neutral third party rather than the vendor itself, giving more trustworthy evidence of its controls.
The raw level of exposure from threats and vulnerabilities that exists before any controls or mitigations are applied.
Checking that data supplied to an application matches expected type, length and format before using it, preventing injection and overflow attacks.
Risk posed by current or former employees, contractors or partners who misuse their legitimate access, whether maliciously or through carelessness.
A review of controls and compliance performed by the organisation's own audit staff, often reporting to an audit committee, to find issues before outsiders do.
Removing the manufacturer's restrictions on a mobile operating system, especially iOS, to gain full control, which also disables built-in protections and app store controls.
Continuously recording every change written to a file system or database in a log, so data can be recovered or replayed to a precise point after a failure.
A hardened, closely monitored host that administrators must connect through to reach systems in a secure zone, providing a single controlled path for management access.
Granting elevated access only when needed for a specific task and automatically removing it afterwards, so privileged rights are not held permanently.
An arrangement where copies of cryptographic keys are held by a trusted third party or internal custodian so encrypted data can be recovered if the original key is lost or legally required.
Running a password through a deliberately slow, repeated hashing process, as in PBKDF2 or bcrypt, so each guess costs attackers far more time in brute-force attempts.
Software or a hardware device that secretly records every keystroke a user types, capturing passwords, messages and other sensitive input for an attacker.
A penetration test where testers receive full details such as network diagrams, source code and credentials, allowing thorough testing in less time.
Giving users, services and processes only the minimum access rights required to do their job, and no more, to limit damage from mistakes or compromise.
A directive to preserve all relevant data and suspend normal deletion when litigation or investigation is anticipated, so evidence is not destroyed.
The final incident response phase, a post-incident review of what happened and how the response went, used to improve plans and controls.
Distributing incoming requests across several servers so no single one is overwhelmed, improving performance and keeping services available if one server fails.
Malicious code hidden in a legitimate program that lies dormant until a specific condition is met, such as a date or an employee's account being deleted, then executes its payload.
A pre-approved, scheduled period, usually at low-usage times, during which changes and updates may be made so that any disruption affects as few users as possible.
Inserting malicious code into the memory space of a running, legitimate process so it executes under that process's identity and avoids detection based on files on disk.
Dividing a network into very small zones, down to individual workloads, with policies controlling traffic between each, so attackers cannot move laterally after a breach.
An architecture where an application is built from many small, independently deployable services that communicate over APIs, limiting the impact of a failure in one.
A government-backed threat actor with extensive funding and skill, typically pursuing espionage, disruption or strategic advantage through long-term, stealthy campaigns.
Assurance that someone cannot credibly deny having sent a message or performed an action, typically provided by digital signatures and reliable audit logs.
An attack where the adversary secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties to eavesdrop on, relay or alter traffic, formerly called man-in-the-middle.
A shared, distributed record of transactions that anyone can view and verify, where entries are chained together with hashes so past records cannot be quietly changed; the basis of blockchain.
The sequence for collecting digital evidence from most to least short-lived, such as CPU cache and RAM before disk and backups, so fragile data is not lost.
A professional, well-resourced criminal group that conducts attacks such as ransomware and fraud primarily for financial gain, often operating like a business.

Splitting a workload across multiple processors or systems at once, improving performance and resilience because a faulty node can be identified and bypassed; in recovery testing, backup systems run alongside production to confirm results.
A penetration test where testers receive some limited information, such as IP ranges or a user account, simulating an attacker with partial insider knowledge.
Using a stolen password hash directly to authenticate to other systems that accept it, typically in Windows NTLM environments, without needing to crack the plaintext password.
Gathering information about a target without directly touching its systems, such as searching public records, social media and DNS registrations.
Trying a few common passwords across many different accounts, rather than many passwords against one account, to avoid triggering lockout thresholds.
Storing privileged account passwords in a secured, audited repository that checks them out to authorised users and often rotates them after use.
An authorised simulated attack in which testers actively exploit vulnerabilities to show how far a real attacker could get and what impact they could have.
A social engineering attack using fraudulent email that impersonates a trusted sender to trick recipients into clicking links, opening attachments or revealing credentials.
An organisation's planned series of simulated lure emails sent to its own staff to measure who clicks or reports, and to target further awareness training.
Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies for the same function so a single vulnerability or failure cannot affect every system at once.
A step-by-step checklist describing exactly how to respond to a specific type of event, such as a malware outbreak, so responses are consistent and fast.
The Zero Trust component that evaluates each access request against rules, identity, device and threat information, and decides whether to grant, deny or revoke access.
Switch-level controls that restrict which devices can use a network port, for example by limiting allowed MAC addresses or requiring 802.1X authentication.
Inventing a believable scenario or false identity, such as posing as IT support or an auditor, to persuade a target to share information or perform an action.
A safeguard designed to stop an incident before it happens, such as a firewall rule, door lock or account permissions that block unauthorised actions outright.
Exploiting a flaw or misconfiguration to gain higher permissions than originally granted, such as moving from a standard user account to administrator or root.
An intermediary that makes requests on behalf of clients, allowing an organisation to filter content, cache data, hide internal addresses and log web activity.
Assessing risk using descriptive ratings, such as low, medium and high for likelihood and impact, based on judgement rather than precise monetary values.
Assessing risk with numerical values, such as asset value, exposure factor and annualised rate of occurrence, to calculate expected monetary loss.
Isolating a suspicious file, device or message so it cannot cause harm or spread while it is analysed, without deleting it.
A flaw where the outcome depends on the timing of events, such as when a resource changes between being checked and being used, letting an attacker slip in an unauthorised action.
Malware that encrypts or locks a victim's files or systems and demands payment for the key, often also threatening to publish stolen data.
Information whose handling is governed by law or industry rules, such as health records, payment card data or personal data, carrying legal penalties if mishandled.
A formal review by a government agency or regulator to verify that an organisation complies with the laws and rules that apply to its industry.
Copying data continuously or frequently to another system or site, so an up-to-date duplicate is available if the primary copy is lost.
The risk that remains after controls and mitigations have been applied, which leadership must accept, transfer or reduce further.
A chart defining which security duties the cloud provider handles and which the customer must handle for each service model, such as IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Reporting a discovered vulnerability privately to the vendor and allowing reasonable time for a fix before making details public.
A privacy right allowing individuals to request that organisations delete their personal data when it is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn.
A contract provision that allows a customer to inspect or have a third party examine a vendor's security controls and records.
Deciding to tolerate a risk without further action because the cost of mitigating it outweighs the likely loss, formally documented by an accountable owner.
The overall amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue to achieve its goals, often described as expansionary, conservative or neutral.
Eliminating a risk entirely by stopping or never starting the activity that causes it, such as dropping a risky product feature.
Reducing a risk's likelihood or impact by applying controls, such as patching, encryption or additional monitoring.
The person accountable for managing a specific risk, including deciding the response and monitoring it over time.
A central document or database listing identified risks along with their likelihood, impact, owner, key indicators and chosen responses.
A defined level at which a specific risk becomes unacceptable and triggers escalation or action.
The acceptable amount of variation from the organisation's overall stance on risk for a particular objective or risk, indicating how much deviation can be absorbed.
Shifting the financial impact of a risk to another party, most commonly by buying cybersecurity insurance or shifting liability to a contractor through an agreement.
Investigating an incident to identify the underlying reason it occurred, not just its symptoms, so the same problem can be prevented from recurring.
An inherently trusted starting point, such as a hardware chip or a top-level certificate authority, from which the trustworthiness of other components or certificates is verified.
Malware that embeds itself deep in the operating system or firmware, often at kernel level, to hide its presence and maintain privileged, persistent control.
Agreed terms defining what a tester or vendor may and may not do during an assessment, including scope, timing, methods and contacts.
Adding a unique random value to each password before hashing it, so identical passwords produce different stored hashes and precomputed rainbow tables become ineffective.
Running code or opening files in a tightly isolated environment so their behaviour can be observed or contained without affecting the host system.
Removing data from storage media so thoroughly that it cannot be recovered, such as by overwriting or cryptographic erase, before reuse or disposal.
A separate network segment between the internet and the internal network that hosts public-facing services, so a compromise there does not give direct internal access; also known as a DMZ.
A documented, approved set of security configuration settings that systems are built to and regularly checked against, so drift can be detected.
A protected, isolated area of a processor that keeps keys and sensitive computations separate from the main operating system, so even a compromised OS cannot read them.
A digital certificate whose issuer is itself rather than a trusted authority; useful for internal testing, but browsers and clients will not trust it by default.
A cloud model where code runs as functions on demand and the provider manages all underlying servers, shifting patching duties away from the customer.
Hardware, software or cloud services used by staff without the knowledge or approval of the IT department, creating unmanaged and unmonitored risk.
Installing an application on a device from outside the official app store, bypassing the vetting and signing checks that would normally catch malicious apps.
Staying alert to one's surroundings and to unusual requests or events, so potential threats such as tailgaters or suspicious messages are noticed in time.
A social engineering attack delivered by SMS text message, luring the recipient to tap a malicious link or call a fraudulent number.
A point-in-time image of a system, virtual machine or storage volume, used to quickly roll back to that exact state after a failed change or corruption.
Malware that secretly monitors a user's activity, such as browsing, location or communications, and sends that information to a third party without consent.
Examining application source code for security flaws without running it, typically with automated tools early in development.
Hiding data inside another, innocent-looking file or medium, such as an image, audio file or network traffic, so that the existence of the hidden message is concealed.
Evaluating the security risks introduced by a vendor's own suppliers and components, not just the vendor itself, before and during a relationship.
Compromising a trusted vendor, service provider or software component so that malicious code or access reaches the real target through a legitimate channel such as an update.
A discussion-based session where team members walk through a hypothetical incident scenario to test plans and roles without touching any real systems.
A continuously updated stream of threat intelligence, such as malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes, used to detect and block known attacks.
Proactively searching through networks and systems for hidden attackers or signs of compromise that automated tools have not flagged.
A Zero Trust goal of limiting what any single user or device can reach, through least privilege and segmentation, so a compromise can affect as little as possible.
Access rules that allow accounts to sign in or use resources only during defined hours, reducing the window for misuse.
Replacing a sensitive value, such as a card number, with a random substitute that has no mathematical relationship to it, while the real value is kept in a separate protected vault.
Confidential business information, such as formulas, processes or customer lists, that gives a competitive advantage and is protected by keeping it secret rather than registering it.
Malware disguised as legitimate, useful software that tricks the user into installing it, then performs hidden malicious actions such as opening a backdoor.
Registering domain names that are slight misspellings of popular sites, such as gooogle.com, to catch users who mistype and serve them phishing pages or malware.
A low-capability threat actor who relies on readily available tools and scripts written by others, often attacking opportunistically without deep technical knowledge.
Ongoing review of a third party's security posture, performance and compliance throughout a contract, rather than only at selection.
Tracking every revision of code, configurations and documents so changes can be reviewed, attributed to an author and rolled back to an earlier known-good state.
Exploiting a hypervisor flaw so code running inside a guest breaks out of its isolation and gains access to the host or to other guests on the same hardware.
Running multiple isolated guest operating systems on one physical host through a hypervisor, which improves resource use but makes hypervisor security critical.
A social engineering attack carried out over a voice call, often with spoofed caller ID, where the attacker poses as a bank, help desk or official to extract information.
A recovery location with some equipment and connectivity in place but not fully current data, balancing cost against a recovery time of hours to days.
Compromising a website that a targeted group is known to visit regularly, so their devices become infected when they browse to the trusted site.
A single certificate that covers every subdomain at one level of a domain, written with an asterisk such as *.example.com, simplifying management but widening the impact if its key is stolen.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks on its own by exploiting vulnerabilities, without needing a user to run it or attach it to a host file.
A vulnerability unknown to the vendor or without an available patch, giving defenders no time to fix it before attackers can exploit it.
